\chapter{Photography, Photos and Permission}
\label{ch:fotografia-foto-permitir}
\hlchaptermodality{405}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can distinguish a photo from photography and understand whether taking photographs is permitted.}

Retrieve the three image words across an ID form and a public sign.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la fotografía]{la fotografía — writing with light}

\label{lesson:ES-C405-fotografia}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to make or do} and \emph{the room}. (\emph{Hacer, la sala}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{fo-to-gra-FEE-a}: the written accent keeps \textbf{í} and \textbf{a} in separate syllables.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la fotografía} means both “photography” and “a photograph.” Its international parts come from Greek \textbf{phôs, phōtós}, “light,” and \textbf{graphía}, “writing or description.” A photograph is, quite literally, writing with light.

Spanish commonly says \textbf{hacer fotografías}, “to take photographs.” The verb is the familiar \textbf{hacer}: Spanish pictures the activity as making photographs.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la fotografía}
  \item \emph{hacer fotografías}
  \item \emph{hacer fotografías en la sala}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \emph{to take photographs}. (\emph{Hacer fotografías}.)

Sources: \href{https://dle.rae.es/fotograf\%C3\%ADa}{DLE: fotografía} and \href{https://dle.rae.es/foto-}{DLE: foto-}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la foto]{la foto — the short word keeps the long word's gender}

\label{lesson:ES-C405-foto}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the photograph} and \emph{the passport}. (\emph{La fotografía, el pasaporte}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la foto} is the everyday short form of \textbf{la fotografía}. It ends in \textbf{-o}, but it remains feminine because the full word is feminine: \textbf{la foto}, never \emph{el foto} for an ordinary photograph.

The two forms overlap, but the short one is especially natural for a physical photo or an ID picture: \textbf{una foto y el pasaporte}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la foto}
  \item \emph{una foto}
  \item \emph{una foto y el pasaporte}
  \item \emph{la foto, la fotografía}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \emph{a photo and the passport}. (\emph{Una foto y el pasaporte}.)

Source: \href{https://dle.rae.es/foto}{DLE: foto}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[permitir]{permitir — let something pass through}

\label{lesson:ES-C405-permitir}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to take photographs in the room}. (\emph{Hacer fotografías en la sala}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{per-mi-TEER}: keep the two \textbf{r} sounds light and stress the final syllable.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{permitir} means “to permit” or “to allow.” It continues Latin \textbf{permittere}, “to let through,” built from \textbf{per-}, “through,” and \textbf{mittere}, “to send or let go.” English \emph{permit} belongs to the same family.

On a public sign, \textbf{está permitido} means “it is permitted,” while \textbf{no está permitido} means “it is not permitted.” Treat that whole sign formula as one useful chunk here.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{permitir}
  \item \emph{está permitido}
  \item \emph{no está permitido}
  \item \emph{no está permitido hacer fotografías en la sala}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \emph{it is not permitted to take photographs}. (\emph{No está permitido hacer fotografías}.)

Source: \href{https://dle.rae.es/permitir}{DLE: permitir}.
\end{tcolorbox}
